Numerical approximation of a reaction-diffusion system

with fast reversible reaction

Robert Eymard 11 1 Université Paris-Est, 77454 Marne-la-Vallée Cédex 2, France; E-mail: Robert.Eymard@univ-mlv.fr,  Danielle Hilhorst 22 2 Laboratoire de Mathématiques, CNRS and Université de Paris-Sud 11, 91405 Orsay Cédex, France; E-mail: Danielle.Hilhorst@math.u-psud.fr,  Michal Olech 33 3 Instytut Matematyczny Uniwersytetu Wroclawskiego, pl. Grunwaldzki 2/4, 50-384 Wroclaw, Polska; Laboratoire de Mathématiques, CNRS Université de Paris-Sud, 91405 Orsay Cédex, France; E-mail: olech@math.uni.wroc.pl.
The preparation of this article has been partially supported by a Marie Curie Transfer of Knowledge Fellowship of the European Community’s Sixth Framework Programme under contract number MTKD-CT-2004-013389

Key words: instantaneous reaction limit, mass-action kinetics, finite volume methods, convergence of approximate solutions, discrete a priori estimates, Kolmogorov’s theorem.

AMS subject classification: 35K45, 35K50, 35K55, 65M12, 65N12, 65N22, 80A30, 92E20.

Abstract

We consider the finite volume approximation of a reaction-diffusion system with fast reversible reaction. We deduce from a priori estimates that the approximate solution converges to the weak solution of the reaction – diffusion problem and satisfies estimates which do not depend on the chemical kinetics factor. It follows that the solution converges to the solution of a nonlinear diffusion problem, as the size of the volume elements and the time steps converge to zero while the kinetic rate tends to infinity.

1 Introduction

In this paper, we consider chemical systems with fast reactions where mean reaction times vary from approximately 10−1410^{-14} second to 1 minute. In particular, reactions that involve bond making or breaking are not likely to occur in less than 10−1310^{-13} second. Moreover, chemical systems almost always involve some elementary reaction steps that are reversible and fast.
The study of reactions with rates that are outside of the time frame of ordinary laboratory operations requires specialized instrumentation, techniques and ways of proceeding (see for example Espenson [4, Chapter 11]). This work tries to give an efficient, quick and cheap way for numerical investigations of such reactions.

In this article, we consider a reversible chemical reaction between mobile species 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B}, that takes place inside a bounded region Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} where d=1,2d=1,2 or 33. If the region is isolated and diffusion is modelled by Fick’s law, this leads to the reaction-diffusion system of partial differential equations

ut=a​Δ​u−α​k​(rA​(u)−rB​(v))​ in ​Ω×(0,T),vt=b​Δ​v+β​k​(rA​(u)−rB​(v))​ in ​Ω×(0,T),\begin{split}u_{t}&=a\Delta u-\alpha k\big(r_{A}(u)-r_{B}(v)\big)\text{\quad in \quad}\Omega\times(0,T),\\ v_{t}&=b\Delta v+\beta k\big(r_{A}(u)-r_{B}(v)\big)\text{\quad in \quad}\Omega\times(0,T),\end{split} (1)

where T>0T>0 and Ω\Omega is a bounded set of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. An example of explicit expressions and values for α,β,k,rA,rB,a,b\alpha,\ \beta,\ k,\ r_{A},\ r_{B},\ a,\ b is given in Section 6. We supplement the system (1) by the homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions

∇u⋅𝒏=∇v⋅𝒏=0 on ∂Ω×(0,T),\nabla u\cdot\boldsymbol{n}=\nabla v\cdot\boldsymbol{n}=0\text{\quad on \quad}\partial\Omega\times(0,T), (2)

and the initial conditions of the form

u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),v⁡(x,0)=v0​(x)​ in ​Ω.u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\ v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\text{\quad in \quad}\Omega. (3)

In the sequel we call the system (1) together with the boundary conditions (2) and the initial conditions (3), Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k}.
For a reversible reaction m​𝒜⇌n​ℬm\mathcal{A}\rightleftharpoons n\mathcal{B} one has α=−m,β=n\alpha=-m,\ \beta=n and the rate functions are of the form rA​(u)=umr_{A}(u)=u^{m} and rB​(v)=vnr_{B}(v)=v^{n}. Further discussion about this motivation and some concrete examples can be found in Érdi and Tóth [9] and Espenson [4].

In practice, especially for ionic or radical reactions, changes due to reaction are often very fast compared to diffusive effects. This corresponds to a large rate constant kk. Bothe and Hilhorst [1] study the limit to an instantaneous reaction. They exploit a natural Lyapunov functional and use compactness arguments to prove that

uk→uandvk→vinL2​(Ω×(0,T)),u^{k}\rightarrow u\quad\text{and}\quad v^{k}\rightarrow v\quad\text{in}\quad L^{2}\big(\Omega\times(0,T)\big),

as kk tends to infinity, where (uk,vk)(u^{k},v^{k}) is the solution of Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k} and the limit (u,v)(u,v) is determined by

rA​(u)=rB​(v)anduα+vβ=w,r_{A}(u)=r_{B}(v)\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{u}{\alpha}+\frac{v}{\beta}=w, (4)

where ww is the unique weak solution of the nonlinear diffusion problem

wt=Δϕ(w)inΩ×(0,T)∂ϕ⁡(w)∂𝒏=0on∂Ω×(0,T)w⁡(x,0)=w0(x):=1αu0(x)+1βv0(x)inΩ,\begin{split}w_{t}&=\Delta\phi(w)\quad\text{in}\quad\Omega\times(0,T)\\ \frac{\partial\phi(w)}{\partial\boldsymbol{n}}&=0\quad\text{on}\quad\partial\Omega\times(0,T)\\ w(x,0)&=w_{0}(x):=\frac{1}{\alpha}u_{0}(x)+\frac{1}{\beta}v_{0}(x)\quad\text{in}\quad\Omega\hskip 3.0pt,\end{split} (5)

with

ϕ:=(aα​id+bβ​η)∘(1α​id+1β​η)−1onℝ+,η=rB−1∘rA.\begin{split}\phi:=\bigg(\frac{a}{\alpha}\text{id}+\frac{b}{\beta}\eta\bigg)&\circ\bigg(\frac{1}{\alpha}\text{id}+\frac{1}{\beta}\eta\bigg)^{-1}\quad\text{on}\quad\mathbb{R}^{+},\\ \eta&=r_{B}^{-1}\circ r_{A}.\end{split} (6)

The identities in (4) can be explained as follows: the first one states that the system is in chemical equilibrium, while the second one defines ww as the quantity that is conserved under the chemical reaction. Given a function ww, the system (4) can be uniquely solved for (u,v)(u,v) if rA,rBr_{A},\,r_{B} are strictly increasing with for instance rA​(ℝ+)⊂rB​(ℝ+)r_{A}(\mathbb{R}^{+})\subset r_{B}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) so that η=rB−1∘rA\eta=r_{B}^{-1}\circ r_{A} is well defined and strictly increasing. Under these assumptions uu is the unique solution of

1α​u+1β​η​(u)=w,\frac{1}{\alpha}u+\frac{1}{\beta}\eta(u)=w,

which gives the explicit representation of uu and vv

u=(1α​id+1β​η)−1​(w),v=η∘(1α​id+1β​η)−1​(w).u=\bigg(\frac{1}{\alpha}\text{id}+\frac{1}{\beta}\eta\bigg)^{-1}\hskip-4.0pt\big(w\big),\quad v=\eta\circ\bigg(\frac{1}{\alpha}\text{id}+\frac{1}{\beta}\eta\bigg)^{-1}\hskip-4.0pt\big(w\big). (7)

We assume the following hypotheses, which we denote by ℋ\mathcal{H}:

  1. 1.

    Let Ω\Omega be an open, connected and bounded subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, where d=1,2d=1,2 or 33, with a smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega,

  2. 2.

    u0​(x),v0​(x)∈L∞​(Ω)u_{0}(x),\ v_{0}(x)\in L^{\infty}(\Omega) and there exist constants U,V>0U,\ V>0 such that 0⩽u0​(x)⩽U0\leqslant u_{0}(x)\leqslant U and 0⩽v0​(x)⩽V0\leqslant v_{0}(x)\leqslant V in Ω\Omega,

  3. 3.

  4. 4.

We recall from Bothe and Hilhorst [1, Section 2] that Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k} has a unique classical solution (uk,vk)(u^{k},v^{k}) on every finite time interval [0,T][0,T], for all nonnegative bounded initial data. By classical solution, we mean a function pair (uk,vk)(u^{k},\,v^{k}) such that uk,vk∈C2,1​(Ω×(0,T])∩C1,0​(Ω¯×(0,T])u^{k},\,v^{k}\in C^{2,1}\big(\Omega\times(0,T]\big)\cap C^{1,0}\big(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,T]\big) with uk,vk∈C⁡([0,T],L2​(Ω))u^{k},v^{k}\in C\big([0,T];\,L^{2}(\Omega)\big) (see also Ladyženskaja, Solonnikov and Ural’ceva [11]).

We remark that every essentially bounded weak solution of Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k}, in the sense of Definition 1.1, is also a classical solution.

This paper is organized as follows. In section 2 we define a finite volume discretisation and an approximate solution (u𝒟k,v𝒟k)(u_{\cal D}^{k},v_{\cal D}^{k}) for Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k}. In section 3 we prove a discrete comparison principle which yields discrete L∞L^{\infty} estimates, and we show the existence and uniqueness of the approximate solution. Section 4 contains technical lemmas used further in the convergence proofs. The convergence of the approximate solution to the classical solution of Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k} in the case of fixed kk is proved in section 5. In section 6 we use a suitable Lyapunov function and we obtain a discrete L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))L^{2}\big(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)\big) estimate, which does not depend on kk. We then apply Kolmogorov’s theorem and deduce the convergence of the approximate solutions to the classical solution of Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k}. Afterwards we show that the approximate solution (u𝒟k,v𝒟k)(u_{\cal D}^{k},v_{\cal D}^{k}) converges to (u,v)(u,v) defined in (7) as kk tends to ∞\infty and the size of the discretisation parameters tends to zero.
In Section 6 we present numerical results obtained with our finite volume scheme, for the reversible dimerisation of oo-phenylenedioxydimethylsilane (2,22,2-dimethyl-1,2,31,2,3-benzodioxasilole) which is a reaction of the type 2​𝒜⇌ℬ2\mathcal{A}\rightleftharpoons\mathcal{B} (see Meyer, Klein and Weiss [12]). On the one hand we compute the approximate solution (u𝒟k,v𝒟k)(u_{\cal D}^{k},v_{\cal D}^{k}) of the solution (uk,vk)(u^{k},v^{k}) of Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k} and on the other hand the numerical approximation w𝒟w_{\cal D} of the solution ww of the problem (5) – (6), and we check that

 ​u𝒟k≈(1α​id+1β​η)−1​(w𝒟)andv𝒟k≈η∘(1α​id+1β​η)−1​(w𝒟)​ \rule{20.0pt}{0.0pt}u_{\cal D}^{k}\approx\bigg(\frac{1}{\alpha}\text{id}+\frac{1}{\beta}\eta\bigg)^{-1}\hskip-4.0pt\big(w_{\cal D}\big)\quad\text{and}\quad v_{\cal D}^{k}\approx\eta\circ\bigg(\frac{1}{\alpha}\text{id}+\frac{1}{\beta}\eta\bigg)^{-1}\hskip-4.0pt\big(w_{\cal D}\big)\rule{20.0pt}{0.0pt}

for kk large enough and size​(𝒟)\hbox{\rm size}\,({\cal D}) small enough.

In what follows we denote by CC, CkC_{k} and CψC_{\psi} positive generic constants which may vary from line to line.

2 The finite volume scheme

The finite volume method has first been developed by engineers in order to study complex, coupled physical problems where the conservation of quantities such as masses, energy or impulsion must be carefully respected by the approximate solution. Another advantage of this method is that a large variety of meshes can be used in the computations. The finite volume methods are particularly well suited for numerical investigations of conservations laws. They are one of the most popular methods among the engineers performing computations for industrial purposes: the modelling of flows in porous media, problems related to oil recovery, questions related to hydrology, such as the numerical approximation of a stationary incompressible Navier – Stokes equations.

For a comprehensive discussion about the finite volume method, we refer to Eymard, Gallouët and Herbin [6] and the references therein.

Following [6], we define a finite volume discretization of QTQ_{T}.

  1. 1.

    The closure of the union of all the control volumes is Ω¯\overline{\Omega}. We denote by mKm_{K} the measure of each volume element KK and

    size​(ℳ)=maxK∈ℳ⁡mk.\hbox{\rm size}\,({\cal M})=\max_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{k}.

3 The approximate solution

In this section we prove the existence and uniqueness of the solution of the system (11). Let us start with a discrete version of the comparison principle.

Proposition 3.1 (Discrete comparison principle).

We suppose that the hypotheses ℋ\mathcal{H} are satisfied. Let 𝒟\cal D be a discretization as in Definition 2.3. Let (uK(0),vK(0))K∈ℳ(u_{K}^{(0)},v_{K}^{(0)})_{K\in{\cal M}} and (u~K(0),v~K(0))K∈ℳ(\tilde{u}_{K}^{(0)},\tilde{v}_{K}^{(0)})_{K\in{\cal M}} be given sequences of real values such that

uK(0)⩽u~K(0)andvK(0)⩽v~K(0),u_{K}^{(0)}\leqslant\tilde{u}_{K}^{(0)}\quad\text{and}\quad v_{K}^{(0)}\leqslant\tilde{v}_{K}^{(0)},

(u~K(n+1),v~K(n+1))K∈ℳ,n∈{0,…,N}(\tilde{u}_{K}^{(n+1)},\tilde{v}_{K}^{(n+1)})_{K\in{\cal M},\ n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}} satisfy the equations (11) with the initial values (uK(0),vK(0))K∈ℳ(u_{K}^{(0)},v_{K}^{(0)})_{K\in{\cal M}} and (u~K(0),v~K(0))K∈ℳ(\tilde{u}_{K}^{(0)},\tilde{v}_{K}^{(0)})_{K\in{\cal M}}, respectively, then for K∈ℳK\in{\cal M} and n∈{0,…,N}n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}

With the notation from Proposition 3.1, we have that

Theorem 3.3.

Let 𝒟=(ℳ,𝒫,ℰ,(tδ(n))n∈{0,…,N+1}){\cal D}=\Big({\cal M},{\cal P},{\cal E},(t_{\delta}^{(n)})_{n\in\{0,\ldots,N+1\}}\Big) be an admissible discretization of QTQ_{T} in the sense of Definition 2.3. We suppose that the hypotheses ℋ\mathcal{H} are satisfied. Let (uK(0),vK(0))K∈ℳ(u_{K}^{(0)},v_{K}^{(0)})_{K\in{\cal M}} be given by (10) and (uK(n+1),vK(n+1))(u_{K}^{(n+1)},v_{K}^{(n+1)}) satisfy (11) for K∈ℳK\in{\cal M} and n∈{0,…,N}n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}. Then

0⩽uK(n+1)⩽U+αβ​Vand0⩽vK(n+1)⩽V+βα​U,0\leqslant u_{K}^{(n+1)}\leqslant U+\frac{\alpha}{\beta}V\quad\text{and}\quad 0\leqslant v_{K}^{(n+1)}\leqslant V+\frac{\beta}{\alpha}U,\ (18)

for all K∈ℳK\in{\cal M} and n∈{0,…,N}\ n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}, where UU and VV are the positive constants from the hypothesis ℋ​ 2\mathcal{H}\,2.

Proof   From Proposition 3.1 we immediately obtain that uK(n+1)u_{K}^{(n+1)} and vK(n+1)v_{K}^{(n+1)} are nonnegative for K∈ℳK\in{\cal M} and n∈{0,…,N}\ n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}. In order to find a discrete upper solution, we consider approximate solutions of the corresponding system of ordinary differential equations. More precisely, we consider sequences (u¯(n))n∈{0,…,N+1}(\bar{u}^{(n)})_{n\in\{0,\ldots,N+1\}}, (v¯(n))n∈{0,…,N+1}(\bar{v}^{(n)})_{n\in\{0,\ldots,N+1\}} (we postpone for a moment the proof that they exist) such that

u¯(0)=U,v¯(0)=V\bar{u}^{(0)}=U,\quad\bar{v}^{(0)}=V

and

u¯(n+1)−u¯(n)=α​k​tδ(n)​(rB​(v¯(n+1))−rA​(u¯(n+1))),v¯(n+1)−v¯(n)=β​k​tδ(n)​(rA​(u¯(n+1))−rB​(v¯(n+1))),\begin{split}\bar{u}^{(n+1)}-\bar{u}^{(n)}&=\alpha k\,t_{\delta}^{(n)}\Big(r_{B}(\bar{v}^{(n+1)}\big)-r_{A}\big(\bar{u}^{(n+1)})\Big),\\ \bar{v}^{(n+1)}-\bar{v}^{(n)}&=\beta k\,t_{\delta}^{(n)}\Big(r_{A}\big(\bar{u}^{(n+1)})-r_{B}(\bar{v}^{(n+1)}\big)\Big),\end{split} (19)

for n∈{0,…,N}n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}. We note that the sequences (u¯(n+1))n∈{0,…,N}(\bar{u}^{(n+1)})_{n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}}, (v¯(n+1))n∈{0,…,N}(\bar{v}^{(n+1)})_{n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}} satisfy (11) with the initial data U,VU,V. Therefore they satisfy the comparison principle from Proposition 3.1 which yields

0⩽u¯(n+1)and0⩽v¯(n+1)for alln∈{0,…,N}.0\leqslant\bar{u}^{(n+1)}\quad\text{and}\quad 0\leqslant\bar{v}^{(n+1)}\quad\text{for all}\quad n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}. (20)

Adding up the first equation of (19) divided by α\alpha and the second one divided by β\beta, we obtain

u¯(n+1)α+v¯(n+1)β=u¯(n)α+v¯(n)β=…=Uα+Vβ.\frac{\bar{u}^{(n+1)}}{\alpha}+\frac{\bar{v}^{(n+1)}}{\beta}=\frac{\bar{u}^{(n)}}{\alpha}+\frac{\bar{v}^{(n)}}{\beta}=\ldots=\frac{U}{\alpha}+\frac{V}{\beta}\enskip.

We deduce from the previous equation and from (20) that

0⩽u¯(n+1)⩽U+αβ​V​ and ​0⩽v¯(n+1)⩽V+βα​U,0\leqslant\bar{u}^{(n+1)}\leqslant U+\frac{\alpha}{\beta}V\text{\quad and\quad}0\leqslant\bar{v}^{(n+1)}\leqslant V+\frac{\beta}{\alpha}U, (21)

for n∈{0,…,N}n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}.  ■\blacksquare

In order to prove the existence of the sequences (u¯(n))n∈{0,…,N+1}(\bar{u}^{(n)})_{n\in\{0,\ldots,N+1\}} and (v¯(n))n∈{0,…,N+1}(\bar{v}^{(n)})_{n\in\{0,\ldots,N+1\}} we use the topological degree theory in finite dimensional spaces. The reader can find basic definitions as well as further informations about this powerful theory in Deimling [3]. An example of the application of this tool to the analysis of finite volume schemes can be found in Eymard, Gallouët, Ghilani and Herbin [5].

With ℱ,𝒢:ℝ2→ℝ2\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2} defined as

ℱ⁡(u¯(n),v¯(n))=(u¯(n),v¯(n)),𝒢⁡(u¯(n),v¯(n))=(α^tδ(n−1)(rA(u¯(n))−rB(v¯(n))),OPEN−β^​tδ(n−1)​(rA​(u¯(n))−rB​(v¯(n)))),\begin{split}\mathcal{F}\big(\bar{u}^{(n)},\bar{v}^{(n)}\big)=&\ \big(\bar{u}^{(n)},\bar{v}^{(n)}\big),\\ \mathcal{G}\big(\bar{u}^{(n)},\bar{v}^{(n)}\big)=&\ \bigg(\hat{\alpha}t_{\delta}^{(n-1)}\Big(r_{A}\big(\bar{u}^{(n)})-r_{B}(\bar{v}^{(n)}\big)\Big),\\ &-\hat{\beta}t_{\delta}^{(n-1)}\Big(r_{A}\big(\bar{u}^{(n)})-r_{B}(\bar{v}^{(n)}\big)\Big)\bigg),\end{split}

we rewrite the system (19) in the form

ℱ⁡(u¯(n+1),v¯(n+1))+𝒢⁡(u¯(n+1),v¯(n+1))=y:=(u¯(n),v¯(n)).\mathcal{F}\big(\bar{u}^{(n+1)},\bar{v}^{(n+1)}\big)+\mathcal{G}\big(\bar{u}^{(n+1)},\bar{v}^{(n+1)}\big)=y:=\big(\bar{u}^{(n)},\bar{v}^{(n)}\big).

Moreover we see that setting 𝒪=B⁡(0,r)⊂ℝ2\mathcal{O}=B(0,r)\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} a ball centered at (0,0)(0,0) with a radius

r>(U+αβ​V)2+(V+βα​U)2r>\sqrt{\big(U+\tfrac{\alpha}{\beta}V\big)^{2}+\big(V+\tfrac{\beta}{\alpha}U\big)^{2}}

we fulfill all the assumptions of Theorem [3, Theorem 3.1, page 16].
For the continuous function ℋ:[0,1]×B⁡(0,r)→ℝ2\mathcal{H}:[0,1]\times B(0,r)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2} given by

ℋ⁡(λ,u¯(n+1),v¯(n+1))=ℱ⁡(u¯(n+1),v¯(n+1))+λ​𝒢​(u¯(n+1),v¯(n+1)),\mathcal{H}(\lambda,\bar{u}^{(n+1)},\bar{v}^{(n+1)})=\mathcal{F}(\bar{u}^{(n+1)},\bar{v}^{(n+1)})+\lambda\mathcal{G}(\bar{u}^{(n+1)},\bar{v}^{(n+1)}),

we see that

d⁡(ℱ+λ​𝒢,B,(u¯(n),v¯(n)))=d⁡(ℋ⁡(λ),B,(u¯(n),v¯(n)))d\big(\mathcal{F}+\lambda\mathcal{G},B,(\bar{u}^{(n)},\bar{v}^{(n)})\big)=d\big(\mathcal{H}(\lambda),B,(\bar{u}^{(n)},\bar{v}^{(n)})\big)

for all λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] and (u¯(n)),(v¯(n))(\overline{u}^{(n)}),\,(\overline{v}^{(n)}) such that 0⩽u¯(n)⩽U−αβ​V0\leqslant\bar{u}^{(n)}\leqslant U-\tfrac{\alpha}{\beta}V and 0⩽v¯(n)⩽V−βα​U0\leqslant\bar{v}^{(n)}\leqslant V-\tfrac{\beta}{\alpha}U for n∈{0,…,N}n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}. On the other hand we deduce from [3, Theorem 3.1, page 16] (d1) that

d⁡(ℋ⁡(0),B,(u¯(n),v¯(n)))=1.d\big(\mathcal{H}(0),B,(\bar{u}^{(n)},\bar{v}^{(n)})\big)=1. (22)

In view of [3, Theorem 3.1, page 16] (d3) and (d4), (22) implies that the equality

ℱ⁡(u¯(n+1),v¯(n+1))+𝒢⁡(u¯(n+1),v¯(n+1))=(u¯(n),v¯(n))\mathcal{F}(\bar{u}^{(n+1)},\bar{v}^{(n+1)})+\mathcal{G}(\bar{u}^{(n+1)},\bar{v}^{(n+1)})=\big(\bar{u}^{(n)},\bar{v}^{(n)}\big)

has a solution or, in other words, that there exists a solution of (19). The uniqueness of this solution immediately follows from Proposition 3.1.

We can prove in the same way the existence and uniqueness of the solution of the system (11). Indeed, we rewrite (11) in the form

ℱ~​((uK(n+1))K∈ℳ,(vK(n+1))K∈ℳ)+𝒢~​((uK(n+1))K∈ℳ,(vK(n+1))K∈ℳ)=((uK(n))K∈ℳ,(vK(n))K∈ℳ),\widetilde{\cal F}\Big((u^{(n+1)}_{K})_{K\in\cal M},(v^{(n+1)}_{K})_{K\in\cal M}\Big)+\widetilde{\cal G}\Big((u^{(n+1)}_{K})_{K\in\cal M},(v^{(n+1)}_{K})_{K\in\cal M}\Big)=\ \Big((u^{(n)}_{K})_{K\in\cal M},(v^{(n)}_{K})_{K\in\cal M}\Big), (23)

where ℱ~,𝒢~:ℝ2​Θ→ℝ2​Θ\widetilde{\cal F},\widetilde{\cal G}:\mathbb{R}^{2\Theta}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2\Theta}, with Θ\Theta the number of control volumes for the discretization 𝒟\cal D, are continuous functions given by

ℱ~​((uK(n))K∈ℳ,(vK(n))K∈ℳ)=((uK(n))K∈ℳ,(vK(n))K∈ℳ),𝒢~​((uK(n))K∈ℳ,(vK(n))K∈ℳ)=(𝒲1,𝒲2),\begin{split}&\widetilde{\cal F}\Big((u^{(n)}_{K})_{K\in\cal M},(v^{(n)}_{K})_{K\in\cal M}\Big)=\Big((u^{(n)}_{K})_{K\in\cal M},(v^{(n)}_{K})_{K\in\cal M}\Big),\\ &\widetilde{\cal G}\Big((u^{(n)}_{K})_{K\in\cal M},(v^{(n)}_{K})_{K\in\cal M}\Big)=\big(\mathcal{W}_{1},\mathcal{W}_{2}\big),\end{split}

where

 𝒲1=−tδ(n)​amK∑L∈𝒩KTK|L(uL(n)−uK(n))+tδ(n−1)α^(rA(uK(n))−rB(vK(n))), \rule{15.0pt}{0.0pt}\mathcal{W}_{1}=-\frac{t_{\delta}^{(n)}a}{m_{K}}\sum_{L\in{\cal N}_{K}}T_{K|L}(u_{L}^{(n)}-u_{K}^{(n)})+t_{\delta}^{(n-1)}\hat{\alpha}\big(r_{A}(u_{K}^{(n)})-r_{B}(v_{K}^{(n)})\big),\rule{15.0pt}{0.0pt}

and where

 𝒲2=−tδ(n)​bmK∑L∈𝒩KTK|L(vL(n)−vK(n))−tδ(n−1)β^(rA(uK(n))−rB(vK(n))). \rule{15.0pt}{0.0pt}\mathcal{W}_{2}=-\frac{t_{\delta}^{(n)}b}{m_{K}}\sum_{L\in{\cal N}_{K}}T_{K|L}(v_{L}^{(n)}-v_{K}^{(n)})-t_{\delta}^{(n-1)}\hat{\beta}\big(r_{A}(u_{K}^{(n)})-r_{B}(v_{K}^{(n)})\big).\rule{15.0pt}{0.0pt}

We set 𝒪~=B⁡(0,R)⊂ℝ2​Θ\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}=B(0,R)\subset\mathbb{R}^{2\Theta} a ball centered at zero with a radius

R>Θ​(U+αβ​V)2+Θ​(V+βα​U)2.R>\sqrt{\Theta\big(U+\tfrac{\alpha}{\beta}V\big)^{2}+\Theta\big(V+\tfrac{\beta}{\alpha}U\big)^{2}}.

Since Θ>1\Theta>1, we deduce from the discrete L∞​(QT)L^{\infty}(Q_{T}) estimate of Theorem 3.3 that the equation (23) does not have any solutions on ∂𝒪~\partial\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}. Applying again [3, Theorem 3.1, page 16] with ℋ~​(λ)=ℱ~+λ​𝒢~\widetilde{\cal H}(\lambda)=\widetilde{\cal F}+\lambda\widetilde{\cal G} and λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] completes the proof of the following result.

Theorem 3.4.

We suppose that the hypotheses ℋ\mathcal{H} are satisfied. Let 𝒟\cal D be a discretization as in Definition 2.3. Let (uK(0),vK(0))K∈ℳ(u_{K}^{(0)},v_{K}^{(0)})_{K\in{\cal M}} be given by (10). Then there exists one and only one sequence

(uK(n+1),vK(n+1))K∈ℳ,n∈{0,…,N},(u_{K}^{(n+1)},v_{K}^{(n+1)})_{K\in{\cal M},\ n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}},

which satisfies (11), with the initial condition (uK(0),vK(0))K∈ℳ(u_{K}^{(0)},v_{K}^{(0)})_{K\in{\cal M}}. ■\blacksquare

4 Convergence proof with kk fixed

We begin with the discrete version of L2​(QT)L^{2}(Q_{T}) estimates of the gradient of the approximate solutions.

Proposition 4.1.

We suppose that the hypotheses ℋ\mathcal{H} are satisfied. Let 𝒟\cal D be a discretization as in Definition 2.3. Let (10) and (11) give the sequences (uK(0),vK(0))K∈ℳ(u_{K}^{(0)},v_{K}^{(0)})_{K\in{\cal M}} and (uK(n+1),vK(n+1))K∈ℳ,n∈{0,…,N}(u_{K}^{(n+1)},v_{K}^{(n+1)})_{K\in{\cal M},\ n\in\{0,\ldots,N\}}, respectively. Then, there exists a constant Ck>0C_{k}>0, which does not depend on 𝒟\cal D, but which depend on all the data of the continuous Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k} (namely, the constants α,β,U,V\alpha,\ \beta,\ U,\ V including kk and the functions rA,rBr_{A},\ r_{B}), such that

 ​12​∑K∈ℳmK​(uK(N+1))2−12​∑K∈ℳmK​(uK(0))2+a​∑n=0Ntδ(n)​∑(K,L)∈ℰTK|L​(uL(n+1)−uK(n+1))2⩽Ck​ \rule{20.0pt}{0.0pt}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{K}\Big(u_{K}^{(N+1)}\Big)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{K}\Big(u_{K}^{(0)}\Big)^{2}+a\sum_{n=0}^{N}t_{\delta}^{(n)}\sum_{(K,L)\in{\cal E}}T_{K|L}\Big(u_{L}^{(n+1)}-u_{K}^{(n+1)}\Big)^{2}\leqslant C_{k}\rule{20.0pt}{0.0pt} (24)

and

 ​12​∑K∈ℳmK​(vK(N+1))2−12​∑K∈ℳmK​(vK(0))2+b​∑n=0Ntδ(n)​∑(K,L)∈ℰTK|L​(vL(n+1)−vK(n+1))2⩽Ck​ \rule{20.0pt}{0.0pt}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{K}\Big(v_{K}^{(N+1)}\Big)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{K}\Big(v_{K}^{(0)}\Big)^{2}+b\sum_{n=0}^{N}t_{\delta}^{(n)}\sum_{(K,L)\in{\cal E}}T_{K|L}\Big(v_{L}^{(n+1)}-v_{K}^{(n+1)}\Big)^{2}\leqslant C_{k}\rule{20.0pt}{0.0pt} (25)

Proof   For the sake of simplicity we only present the proof for the uu-component. We multiply the first equation in the finite volume scheme (11) by uK(n+1)u_{K}^{(n+1)} and sum the result over all K∈ℳK\in\cal M and over all n∈{0,…,N}n\in\{0,\ldots,N\} to obtain

𝒮1+𝒮2+𝒮3=0,\mathcal{S}_{1}+\mathcal{S}_{2}+\mathcal{S}_{3}=0, (26)

where

𝒮1=∑n=0N∑K∈ℳmK​(uK(n+1)−uK(n))​uK(n+1),\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{1}=\sum_{n=0}^{N}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{K}\Big(u_{K}^{(n+1)}-u_{K}^{(n)}\Big)u_{K}^{(n+1)},
𝒮2=−a∑n=0Ntδ(n)∑K∈ℳ∑L∈𝒩KTK|L(uL(n+1)−uK(n+1))uK(n+1),\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{2}=-a\sum_{n=0}^{N}t_{\delta}^{(n)}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}\sum_{L\in{\cal N}_{K}}T_{K|L}\Big(u_{L}^{(n+1)}-u_{K}^{(n+1)}\Big)u_{K}^{(n+1)},
𝒮3=α^​∑n=0Ntδ(n)​∑K∈ℳ(rA​(uK(n+1))−rB​(vK(n+1)))​uK(n+1).\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{3}=\hat{\alpha}\sum_{n=0}^{N}t_{\delta}^{(n)}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}\Big(r_{A}\big(u_{K}^{(n+1)}\big)-r_{B}\big(v_{K}^{(n+1)}\big)\Big)u_{K}^{(n+1)}.

Since

(uK(n+1))2−uK(n)​uK(n+1)=12​(uK(n+1))2−12​(uK(n))2+12​(uK(n+1)−uK(n))2,\Big(u_{K}^{(n+1)}\Big)^{2}-u_{K}^{(n)}u_{K}^{(n+1)}=\frac{1}{2}\Big(u_{K}^{(n+1)}\Big)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\Big(u_{K}^{(n)}\Big)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\Big(u_{K}^{(n+1)}-u_{K}^{(n)}\Big)^{2},

we deduce that

𝒮1=12​∑n=0N∑K∈ℳmK​((uK(n+1))2−(uK(n))2)+12​∑n=0N∑K∈ℳmK​(uK(n+1)−uK(n))2⩾12​∑n=0N∑K∈ℳmK​((uK(n+1))2−(uK(n))2),\mathcal{S}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=0}^{N}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{K}\bigg(\Big(u_{K}^{(n+1)}\Big)^{2}-\Big(u_{K}^{(n)}\Big)^{2}\bigg)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=0}^{N}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{K}\Big(u_{K}^{(n+1)}-u_{K}^{(n)}\Big)^{2}\\ \geqslant\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=0}^{N}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{K}\bigg(\Big(u_{K}^{(n+1)}\Big)^{2}-\Big(u_{K}^{(n)}\Big)^{2}\bigg), (27)

All the terms in the sum on nn on the right hand side of (27) simplify except for the first and the last ones. We have that

𝒮1⩾12​∑K∈ℳmK​(uK(N+1))2−12​∑K∈ℳmK​(uK(0))2.\mathcal{S}_{1}\geqslant\frac{1}{2}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{K}\Big(u_{K}^{(N+1)}\Big)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{K}\Big(u_{K}^{(0)}\Big)^{2}. (28)

We can perform a discrete integration by parts to obtain

𝒮2=a​∑n=0Ntδ(n)​∑(K,L)∈ℰTK|L​(uL(n+1)−uK(n+1))2.\mathcal{S}_{2}=a\sum_{n=0}^{N}t_{\delta}^{(n)}\sum_{(K,L)\in{\cal E}}T_{K|L}\Big(u_{L}^{(n+1)}-u_{K}^{(n+1)}\Big)^{2}. (29)

Finally we use the hypothesis ℋ​ 4\mathcal{H}\,4 and the inequalities in (18) to estimate the last term, namely

−𝒮3⩽α^​∑n=0Ntδ(n)​∑K∈ℳmK​(rA​(U+αβ​V)+rB​(V+βα​U))​(U+αβ​V)⩽α​k​C​∑n=0Ntδ(n)​∑K∈ℳmK=α​k​C​|Ω|​T,-\mathcal{S}_{3}\leqslant\hat{\alpha}\sum_{n=0}^{N}t_{\delta}^{(n)}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{K}\Big(r_{A}\big(U+\frac{\alpha}{\beta}V\big)+r_{B}\big(V+\frac{\beta}{\alpha}U\big)\Big)\big(U+\frac{\alpha}{\beta}V\big)\\ \leqslant\alpha kC\sum_{n=0}^{N}t_{\delta}^{(n)}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{K}=\alpha kC|\Omega|T, (30)

with some positive constant CC.

Identities (26) and (29) together with the inequalities (28) and (30) immediately give (24). Since the argument in the case of the vv-component is similar, we omit the proof.  ■\blacksquare

4.1 Space and time translates of approximate solutions

We now turn to the space translates estimates. We use here methods which have been presented for example by Eymard, Gutnic and Hilhorst [8] and by Eymard, Gallouët, Hilhorst and Slimane [7]. The results of the current and the next subsection together with the technical Proposition 7.2 will imply the relative compactness of the sequence of approximate solutions.

Proposition 4.2 (Space translates estimates).

We assume that

  1. 1.

    𝒟=(ℳ,ℰ,(xK)K∈𝒯,(t(n))n∈{0,…,N+1}){\cal D}=\Big({\cal M},{\cal E},(x_{K})_{K\in{\cal T}},(t^{(n)})_{n\in\{0,\ldots,N+1\}}\Big) is an admissible discretization of QTQ_{T} in the sense of Definition 2.3,

  2. 2.

    the hypotheses ℋ\mathcal{H} and assumptions (36) are satisfied,

  3. 3.

    the functions (u𝒟CLOSE(u_{\cal D} and OPENv𝒟)v_{\cal D}) are derived from the scheme (10) – (11) and given by the formulas (12).

Then there exists a positive constant CkC_{k}, which does not depend on 𝒟\cal D, but depends on all the data of the continuous Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k}, including kk, such that

 ​∫0T∫Ωξ(u𝒟​(x+ξ,t)−u𝒟​(x,t))2​d​x​d​t⩽Ck​|ξ|​(2​size​(𝒟)+|ξ|), \rule{15.0pt}{0.0pt}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega_{\xi}}\big(u_{\cal D}(x+\xi,t)-u_{\cal D}(x,t)\big)^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}t\leqslant C_{k}|\xi|\big(2\,\hbox{\rm size}\,({\cal D}\big)+|\xi|),\rule{15.0pt}{0.0pt} (31)

and

OPEN ​∫0T∫Ωξ(v𝒟​(x+ξ,t)−v𝒟​(x,t))2​d​x​d​t⩽Ck​|ξ|​(2​size​(𝒟))+|ξ|), \rule{15.0pt}{0.0pt}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega_{\xi}}\big(v_{\cal D}(x+\xi,t)-v_{\cal D}(x,t)\big)^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}t\leqslant C_{k}|\xi|\big(2\,\hbox{\rm size}\,({\cal D})\big)+|\xi|),\rule{15.0pt}{0.0pt} (32)

for all ξ∈ℝd\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and for Ωξ\Omega_{\xi} defined as in Proposition 7.2.

Proof   Inequalities (31) and (32) follow from the estimates (24) and (25), respectively. We refer to [6, Lemma 3.3] for a details.  ■\blacksquare

Proposition 4.3 (Time translates estimates).

Let the assumptions of Proposition 4.2 are satisfied. Then, there exists some constant Ck>0C_{k}>0, which does not depend on 𝒟\cal D, but which depend on all the data including kk, such that

 ​∫Ω×(0,T−τ)(u𝒟​(x,t+τ)−u𝒟​(x,t))2​d​x​d​t⩽Ck​(size​(𝒟)+τ)​ \rule{20.0pt}{0.0pt}\int_{\Omega\times(0,T-\tau)}\big(u_{\cal D}(x,t+\tau)-u_{\cal D}(x,t)\big)^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}t\leqslant C_{k}\big(\hbox{\rm size}\,({\cal D})+\tau\big)\rule{20.0pt}{0.0pt} (33)

and

 ​∫Ω×(0,T−τ)(v𝒟​(x,t+τ)−v𝒟​(x,t))2​d​x​d​t⩽Ck​(size​(𝒟)+τ), \rule{20.0pt}{0.0pt}\int_{\Omega\times(0,T-\tau)}\big(v_{\cal D}(x,t+\tau)-v_{\cal D}(x,t)\big)^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}t\leqslant C_{k}\big(\hbox{\rm size}\,({\cal D})+\tau\big),\rule{20.0pt}{0.0pt} (34)

for all τ∈(0,T)\tau\in(0,T).

Proof   In order to apply Lemma 7.1 (see appendix), we follow the same steps as in [8, Lemma 5.5]. The only difference appear in the nonlinear part of the equations. However, these can be easily estimated using the regularity properties of functions rA​(⋅)r_{A}(\cdot) and rB​(⋅)r_{B}(\cdot), as well as L∞L^{\infty} estimates (18) in Theorem 3.3. ■\blacksquare

4.2 Convergence proof

In this section, we state convergence results with kk fixed. This differs from next section where we will introduce additional hypotheses about the nonlinear reaction terms and obtain convergence results which permit us to pass to the limit as k→∞k\rightarrow\infty.

Theorem 4.4.

We suppose that the hypotheses ℋ\mathcal{H} are satisfied. Let (u𝒟,v𝒟)(u_{{\cal D}},v_{{\cal D}}) be the approximate solution defined by (10), (11) and (12). There exist a pair of functions (uk,vk)(u^{k},v^{k}) and a sequence (u𝒟m,v𝒟m)m∈ℕ(u_{{\cal D}_{m}},v_{{\cal D}_{m}})_{m\in\mathbb{N}} of (u𝒟,v𝒟)(u_{{\cal D}},v_{{\cal D}}) such that

(u𝒟m,v𝒟m)m∈ℕ​ converges to ​(uk,vk)∈(L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω)))2(u_{{\cal D}_{m}},v_{{\cal D}_{m}})_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\mbox{~~converges to~~}(u^{k},v^{k})\in\big(L^{2}\big(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)\big)\big)^{2}

strongly in L2​(QT)L^{2}\big(Q_{T}\big) as size​(𝒟m)\hbox{\rm size}\,({\cal D}_{m}) tends to zero. The function pair (uk,vk)(u^{k},v^{k}) is a weak solution of Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k} in the sense of Definition 1.1.

Since Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k} is a uniformly parabolic system, (uk,vk)(u^{k},v^{k}) must coincide with the unique classical solution of Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k} . This immediately yields the following result.

Corollary 4.5.

The pair (u𝒟,v𝒟)(u_{{\cal D}},v_{{\cal D}}) converges to the unique classical solution (uk,vk)(u^{k},v^{k}) of Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k} as size​(𝒟)\hbox{\rm size}\,({\cal D}) tends to zero.  ■\blacksquare

Proof of Theorem 4.4   In view of the estimates (31), (33) and Proposition 7.2 which is a consequence of the Fréchet–Kolmogorov Theorem [2, Theorem IV.25, page 72], we deduce the relative compactness of the set (u𝒟)\big(u_{{\cal D}}\big) so that there exists a sequence of (u𝒟m)m=1∞\big(u_{{\cal D}_{m}}\big)_{m=1}^{\infty} and a function 𝒰k{\cal U}_{k}, such that u𝒟m→𝒰ku_{{\cal D}_{m}}\rightarrow{\cal U}_{k} strongly in L2​(QT)L^{2}(Q_{T}) and weakly in L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))L^{2}\big(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)\big), as m→∞m\rightarrow\infty.

The same conclusion holds for the vv-component. Indeed, the inequalities (32) and (34) permit to apply the compactness result in Proposition 7.2 for the sequence (v𝒟m)m=1∞\big(v_{{\cal D}_{m}}\big)_{m=1}^{\infty}. There exists a function 𝒱k{\cal V}_{k} such that v𝒟m→𝒱kv_{{\cal D}_{m}}\rightarrow{\cal V}_{k} strongly in L2​(QT)L^{2}(Q_{T}) and weakly in L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))L^{2}\big(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)\big) as m→∞m\rightarrow\infty.

Next we show that (𝒰kCLOSE(\mathcal{U}_{k}, OPEN𝒱k)\mathcal{V}_{k}) is a weak solution of Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k}, in the sense of Definition 1.1. Since the proof for the vv-component is similar, we only present here the detailed proof in case of the uu-component.
Let ψ∈Ψ\psi\in\Psi, where Ψ\Psi is the class of test functions from Definition 1.1. We multiply the first equation of (11) by ψ⁡(xK,t(n))\psi(x_{K},t^{(n)}), where ψ∈Ψ\psi\in\Psi. Then we sum over all K∈ℳK\in\cal M and n∈{0​…​N−1}n\in\{0\ldots N-1\} to obtain

𝒯1​mu−𝒯2​mu+𝒯3​mu=0,{\cal T}_{1m}^{u}-{\cal T}_{2m}^{u}+{\cal T}_{3m}^{u}=0,

where

𝒯1​mu\displaystyle{\cal T}_{1m}^{u} =∑n=0N−1∑K∈ℳmK​(uK(n+1)−uK(n))​ψ​(xK,t(n)),\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}m_{K}\big(u_{K}^{(n+1)}-u_{K}^{(n)}\big)\psi(x_{K},t^{(n)}),

and

=\displaystyle= α^​∑n=0N−1∑K∈ℳ∫t(n)t(n+1)∫K(rA​(uK(n+1))−rB​(vK(n+1)))​ψ​(xK,t(n))​d​x​d​t\displaystyle\,\hat{\alpha}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\sum_{K\in{\cal M}}\int_{t^{(n)}}^{t^{(n+1)}}\int_{K}\Big(r_{A}(u_{K}^{(n+1)})-r_{B}(v_{K}^{(n+1)})\Big)\psi(x_{K},t^{(n)})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}t

Corollary 5.5.

∫Ω×(0,T−τ)(w𝒟​(x,t+τ)−w𝒟​(x,t))2​d​x​d​t⩽C⁡(size​(𝒟)+τ),\int_{\Omega\times(0,T-\tau)}\big(w_{\cal D}(x,t+\tau)-w_{\cal D}(x,t)\big)^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}t\leqslant C\big(\hbox{\rm size}\,({\cal D})+\tau\big), (43)

5.2 The limit as s​i​z​e​(𝒟)size(\cal D) tends to zero and kk tends to infinity

We state below the main convergence results of this paper, first only letting the size of the volume elements and the time steps tend to zero, and then also letting the kinetic rate tend to infinity.

Proposition 5.6.

We suppose that the hypotheses ℋ\mathcal{H} are satisfied. Let k>0k>0 be arbitrary and let (uk,vk)∈(L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω)))2(u^{k},\,v^{k})\in\Big(L^{2}\big(0,T;\,H^{1}(\Omega)\big)\Big)^{2} be the unique classical solution of Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k}. Then the sequence (u𝒟k,v𝒟k)(u^{k}_{{\cal D}},\,v^{k}_{{\cal D}}) of approximate solutions of Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k} given by (10), (11) and (12) converges strongly in (L2​(QT))2\Big(L^{2}\big(Q_{T}\big)\Big)^{2} to (uk,vk)(u^{k},\,v^{k}) as size​(𝒟)→0\hbox{\rm size}\,({\cal D})\rightarrow 0. In particular, the sequence w𝒟k=1α​u𝒟k+1β​v𝒟k\displaystyle w^{k}_{{\cal D}}=\frac{1}{\alpha}u^{k}_{{\cal D}}+\frac{1}{\beta}v^{k}_{{\cal D}} converges strongly in L2​(QT)L^{2}\big(Q_{T}\big) to the function wk=1α​uk+1β​vk\displaystyle w^{k}=\frac{1}{\alpha}u^{k}+\frac{1}{\beta}v^{k} as size​(𝒟)→0\hbox{\rm size}\,({\cal D})\rightarrow 0 and there exist positive constants C1,C2C_{1},\,C_{2} which do not depend on kk, such that

k​∫Ω×(0,T)(rA​(uk)−rB​(vk))2​d​x⩽C1,\displaystyle k\int_{\Omega\times(0,T)}\big(r_{A}(u^{k})-r_{B}(v^{k})\big)^{2}\,\text{d}x\leqslant C_{1}, (44)
∫Ωξ×(0,T)(wk​(x+ξ,t)−wk​(x,t))2​d​x​d​t⩽C2​|ξ|2,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega_{\xi}\times(0,T)}\big(w^{k}(x+\xi,t)-w^{k}(x,t)\big)^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}t\leqslant C_{2}|\xi|^{2}, (45)
∫Ω×(0,T−τ)(wk​(x,t+τ)−wk​(x,t))2​d​x​d​t⩽C2​τ,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega\times(0,T-\tau)}\big(w^{k}(x,t+\tau)-w^{k}(x,t)\big)^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}t\leqslant C_{2}\tau, (46)

where τ∈(0,T),ξ∈ℝd\tau\in(0,T),\ \xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and Ωξ={x∈ℝd,[x,x+ξ]⊂Ω}\Omega_{\xi}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},[x,x+\xi]\subset\Omega\}.

Proof   To prove the result we use Corollary 5.5. The method of proof is similar to that of Theorem 4.4.  ■\blacksquare

It is now possible to pass to the limit as k→+∞k\rightarrow+\infty.

Theorem 5.7.

Let (u𝒟k,v𝒟k)\big(u_{\mathcal{D}}^{k},\,v_{\mathcal{D}}^{k}\big) be the sequence of approximate solutions of Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k}, defined by (10), (11) and (12). Then

u𝒟k⟶(1α​id+1β​η)−1​(w)u^{k}_{\mathcal{D}}\longrightarrow\bigg(\frac{1}{\alpha}\text{id}+\frac{1}{\beta}\eta\bigg)^{-1}\!\!\!(w)

and

v𝒟k⟶η∘(1α​id+1β​η)−1​(w)v^{k}_{\mathcal{D}}\longrightarrow\eta\circ\bigg(\frac{1}{\alpha}\text{id}+\frac{1}{\beta}\eta\bigg)^{-1}\!\!\!(w)

as size​(𝒟)→0\hbox{\rm size}\,(\mathcal{D})\rightarrow 0 and kk tends to ∞\infty, where η=rB−1∘rA\eta=r_{B}^{-1}\circ r_{A} and where ww is the unique weak solution of the problem (5) – (6).

Proof   Let w𝒟k=1α​u𝒟k+1β​v𝒟k\displaystyle w^{k}_{{\cal D}}=\frac{1}{\alpha}u^{k}_{{\cal D}}+\frac{1}{\beta}v^{k}_{{\cal D}}. The estimates from Corollary 5.5, which are uniform with respect to kk, permit to apply Proposition 7.2. As a consequence we deduce the relative compactness in L2​(QT)L^{2}(Q_{T}) of the sequence {w𝒟k}\{w^{k}_{{\cal D}}\}. Then there exist a function w∈L2​(QT)w\in L^{2}(Q_{T}) and a subsequence {w𝒟mki}\{w^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}}\} such that w𝒟mkiw^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}} converges to ww strongly in L2​(QT)L^{2}(Q_{T}) as kik_{i} tends to infinity and s​i​z​e​(𝒟m)size({\cal D}_{m}) tends to zero. Theorem 3.3 implies that ww is nonnegative and bounded in QTQ_{T}. The inequality (38), namely

ki​‖rA​(u𝒟mki)−rB​(v𝒟mki)‖L2​(QT)2⩽C{k_{i}}\big\|r_{A}(u^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}})-r_{B}(v^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}})\big\|^{2}_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}\leqslant C

where the positive constant CC is independent of kik_{i} and s​i​z​e​(𝒟m)size({\cal D}_{m}), implies that

rA​(u𝒟mki)−rB​(v𝒟mki)→0inL2​(QT),r_{A}(u^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}})-r_{B}(v^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}})\rightarrow 0\quad\text{in}\quad L^{2}(Q_{T}),

and consequently almost everywhere, as kik_{i} tends to infinity. Then

v𝒟mki=η⁡(u𝒟mki)+e𝒟mki,v^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}}=\eta(u^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}})+e^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}},

where η⁡(s)=rB−1​(rA​(s))\eta(s)=r^{-1}_{B}\big(r_{A}(s)\big) and e𝒟mkie^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}} tends to zero almost everywhere as s​i​z​e​(𝒟m)size({\cal D}_{m}) tends to zero and kik_{i} tends to infinity. In view of the hypotheses ℋ​ 4\mathcal{H}\,4 the function η⁡(s)\eta(s) is well defined on [0,∞)[0,\infty). Moreover,

H⁡(u𝒟mki)=w𝒟mki−1β​e𝒟mki→wa.e. inQT,H(u^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}})=w^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}}-\frac{1}{\beta}e^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}}\rightarrow w\quad\text{a.e.\ in}\quad Q_{T},

where H⁡(s)=1α​s+1β​η​(s)\displaystyle H(s)=\frac{1}{\alpha}s+\frac{1}{\beta}\eta(s). Hypotheses ℋ​ 4\mathcal{H}\,4 ensures that the function H⁡(s)H(s) has the continuous inverse function. Then Lebesgue’s dominated convergence theorem implies that there exists a function pair (u~,v~)∈(L2​(QT))2(\tilde{u},\,\tilde{v})\in\big(L^{2}(Q_{T})\big)^{2}

u𝒟mki→u~andv𝒟mki→v~inL2​(QT)u^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}}\rightarrow\tilde{u}\quad\text{and}\quad v^{k_{i}}_{{\cal D}_{m}}\rightarrow\tilde{v}\quad\text{in}\quad L^{2}(Q_{T}) (47)

as s​i​z​e​(𝒟m)size({\cal D}_{m}) tends to zero and kik_{i} tends to infinity.
Next we identify the limit pair (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\,\tilde{v}). Let w¯\overline{w} be the solution of the problem (5) – (6) and the functions u¯\overline{u} and v¯\overline{v} are defined as in (7), namely

u¯=(1α​id+1β​η)−1​(w¯),v¯=η∘(1α​id+1β​η)−1​(w¯).\overline{u}=\bigg(\frac{1}{\alpha}\text{id}+\frac{1}{\beta}\eta\bigg)^{-1}\hskip-4.0pt\big(\overline{w}\big),\quad\overline{v}=\eta\circ\bigg(\frac{1}{\alpha}\text{id}+\frac{1}{\beta}\eta\bigg)^{-1}\hskip-4.0pt\big(\overline{w}\big).

Let ε>0\varepsilon>0 be arbitrary. We have that

 ​‖u¯−u~‖L2​(QT)⩽‖u¯−uki‖L2​(QT)+‖uki−u𝒟mki‖L2​(QT)+‖u𝒟mki−u~‖L2​(QT)​ .\rule{20.0pt}{0.0pt}\big\|\overline{u}-\tilde{u}\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}\leqslant\big\|\overline{u}-u^{k_{i}}\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}+\big\|u^{k_{i}}-u_{\mathcal{D}_{m}}^{k_{i}}\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}+\big\|u_{\mathcal{D}_{m}}^{k_{i}}-\tilde{u}\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}\rule{5.0pt}{0.0pt}.

From (47) we deduce that there exists k0k_{0} and δ0\delta_{0} such that, for all ki≥k0k_{i}\geq k_{0} and all s​i​z​e​(𝒟m)≤δ0size({\cal D}_{m})\leq\delta_{0}, the last term of the inequality above is less then ε/3\varepsilon/3. From Theorem 1 in [1] there exists some k¯0{{\bar{k}}_{0}}, such that for all ki>k¯0{k_{i}}>{\bar{k}}_{0}, ‖u¯−uki‖L2​(QT)⩽ε/3\big\|\overline{u}-u^{k_{i}}\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}\leqslant\varepsilon/3. Then, fixing ki=max⁡(k0,k¯0)k_{i}=\max(k_{0},{\bar{k}}_{0}), we can take s​i​z​e​(𝒟m)≤δ0size({\cal D}_{m})\leq\delta_{0} small enough so that by Proposition 5.6 ‖uki−u𝒟mki‖L2​(QT)⩽ε/3\big\|u^{k_{i}}-u_{\mathcal{D}_{m}}^{k_{i}}\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}\leqslant\varepsilon/3.
Since the argument for the vv-component is similar, this completes the proof.  ■\blacksquare

6 Numerical example

In this section we give an example of an application of the finite volume scheme (11) in one space dimension.
For the numerical experiments we choose the reaction of the reversible dimerisation of oo-phenylenedioxydimethylsilane (2,22,2-dimethyl-1,2,31,2,3-benzodioxasilole) which has been studied by 1H NMR spectroscopy. The kinetics of this reaction can be described quantitatively by a bimolecular lO-ring formation reaction and a monomolecular backreaction (for further details we refer to Meyer, Klein and Weiss [12]).
Since the reaction is of the type 2​𝒜⇌ℬ2\mathcal{A}\rightleftharpoons\mathcal{B}, the reaction terms take the form

rA​(u)=k1​u2andrB​(v)=k2​v.r_{A}(u)=k_{1}u^{2}\quad\text{and}\quad r_{B}(v)=k_{2}v.

Moreover α=2\alpha=2 and β=1\beta=1. For this particular process benzene was chosen as a solvent. Then it was possible to estimate rate constants for both reactions at the temperature T=298​KT=298K,

k1≈1,072⋅10−4​L2​mol−2andk2≈2,363⋅10−6​L2​mol−2k_{1}\approx 1,072\cdot 10^{-4}\text{L}^{2}\text{mol}^{-2}\quad\text{and}\quad k_{2}\approx 2,363\cdot 10^{-6}\text{L}^{2}\text{mol}^{-2}

and diffusion coefficients

a≈1,579⋅10−9​m2​s−1andb≈1,042⋅10−9​m2​s−1.a\approx 1,579\cdot 10^{-9}\text{m}^{2}\text{s}^{-1}\quad\text{and}\quad b\approx 1,042\cdot 10^{-9}\text{m}^{2}\text{s}^{-1}.

In the experiment we set k=1k=1 for the chemical kinetics factor. We remark that it is equivalent to the situation when coefficients a,b,k1a,\ b,\ k_{1} and k2k_{2} are of order 11 and kk is of order 10410^{4}. In fact, we can multiply the system (1) by 10910^{9} and change the time scale as t↦109​tt\mapsto 10^{9}t. However the above reasoning is formally correct and shows in an explicit way the order of the kinetics factor kk; in our example we decided to keep constants in the form given by the spectroscopic analysis.

Figure 1 shows the initial conditions u0​(x)u_{0}(x) and v0​(x)v_{0}(x), defined as

u0​(x)={0 for ​x∈[0,0.03]12​sin⁡(50​π7​(x−0.03)) for ​x∈[0.03,0.1],u_{0}(x)=\begin{cases}0&\text{ for }x\in[0,0.03]\\ \frac{1}{2}\sin\Big(\frac{50\pi}{7}(x-0.03)\Big)&\text{ for }x\in[0.03,0.1],\end{cases} (48)

and

v0​(x)={14​cos⁡(50​π7​x) for ​x∈[0,0.07],0 for ​x∈[0.07,0.1]v_{0}(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{4}\cos\Big(\frac{50\pi}{7}x\Big)&\text{ for }x\in[0,0.07],\\ 0&\text{ for }x\in[0.07,0.1]\end{cases} (49)

On Figures 3 and 5 we see the time evolution of the solution (u𝒟k,v𝒟k)\big(u_{{\cal D}}^{k},v_{{\cal D}}^{k}\big) until the times Tmax1=105​[s]T_{\text{max}}^{1}=10^{5}\ [s] and Tmax2=1011​[s]T_{\text{max}}^{2}=10^{11}\ [s], respectively. Then we follow the evolution of the solution w𝒟w_{{\cal D}} of the nonlinear diffusion problem (5) – (6) for initial condition deduced from that used in the reaction – diffusion Problem 𝒫k\mathcal{P}^{k}. We have used a uniform mesh with h=0,002h=0,002 and initial time step tδ=10−8t_{\delta}=10^{-8} to obtain the approximate solution (u𝒟k,v𝒟k)\big(u_{{\cal D}}^{k},v_{{\cal D}}^{k}\big) and tδ=10−6t_{\delta}=10^{-6} to obtain the approximate solution w𝒟w_{{\cal D}}to the nonlinear diffusion problem.

We can use the approximate solution w𝒟w_{{\cal D}} and the formulas (7) to define functions u𝒟wu_{{\cal D}}^{w} and v𝒟wv_{{\cal D}}^{w}. Indeed, let

u𝒟w=h⁡(w𝒟)andv𝒟w=g⁡(h⁡(w𝒟)),u_{{\cal D}}^{w}=h\big(w_{{\cal D}}\big)\quad\text{and}\quad v_{{\cal D}}^{w}=g\big(h\big(w_{{\cal D}}\big)\big),

where

h⁡(y)=12​((α​k1β​k2)2+y​4​k2β​k1−α​k2β​k1)h(y)=\frac{1}{2}\bigg(\sqrt{\Big(\frac{\alpha k_{1}}{\beta k_{2}}\Big)^{2}+y\,\frac{4k_{2}}{\beta k_{1}}}-\frac{\alpha k_{2}}{\beta k_{1}}\bigg) (50)

and

g⁡(h)=h​aα+h2​b​k1β​k2.g(h)=h\,\frac{a}{\alpha}+h^{2}\,\frac{bk_{1}}{\beta k_{2}}\hskip 3.0pt. (51)

Proceeding in the similar way as in the proof of Theorem 5.7, we write for the uu-component that

‖u𝒟k−h⁡(w𝒟)‖L2​(QT)⩽‖u𝒟k−uk‖L2​(QT)+‖uk−h⁡(w)‖L2​(QT)+‖h⁡(w)−h⁡(w𝒟)‖L2​(QT).\big\|u_{{\cal D}}^{k}-h(w_{{\cal D}})\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}\leqslant\big\|u_{{\cal D}}^{k}-u^{k}\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}\\ +\big\|u^{k}-h(w)\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}+\big\|h(w)-h(w_{{\cal D}})\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}. (52)

We simultaneously pass to the limit as size​(𝒟)→0\hbox{\rm size}\,({\cal D})\rightarrow 0 and k→∞k\rightarrow\infty. From Theorem 5.7 we immediately deduce that the first term on the right hand side of (52) tends to zero. The same conclusion holds for the two other terms. Indeed, [1, Theorem 1, Sec. 3] implies that ‖uk−h⁡(w)‖L2​(QT)\big\|u^{k}-h(w)\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})} tends to zero as k→∞k\rightarrow\infty. Moreover, [7, Theorem 5.1] yields that ‖w−w𝒟‖L2​(QT)→0\big\|w-w_{{\cal D}}\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}\rightarrow 0 as size​(𝒟)→0\hbox{\rm size}\,({\cal D})\rightarrow 0 and since the function hh is well defined and continuous, we conclude that for every small ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exist 𝒟{\cal D} small enough and kk large enough so that

‖u𝒟k−h⁡(w𝒟)‖L2​(QT)⩽ε.\big\|u_{{\cal D}}^{k}-h(w_{{\cal D}})\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}\leqslant\varepsilon.

We proceed in the same way to show that for every small ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exist 𝒟{\cal D} small enough and kk large enough so that

‖v𝒟k−g⁡(h⁡(w𝒟))‖L2​(QT)⩽ε.\big\|v_{{\cal D}}^{k}-g(h(w_{{\cal D}}))\big\|_{L^{2}(Q_{T})}\leqslant\varepsilon.

The results from our numerical experiment agree with above analysis, since

maxx∈Ω⁡|u𝒟k​(x,Tmax1)−h⁡(w𝒟)​(x,Tmax1)|∞≃4,74⋅10−3,\displaystyle\max_{x\in\Omega}\Big|u_{{\cal D}}^{k}(x,T_{\text{max}}^{1})-h(w_{{\cal D}})(x,T_{\text{max}}^{1})\Big|_{\infty}\simeq 4,74\cdot 10^{-3},
maxx∈Ω⁡|v𝒟k​(x,Tmax1)−g⁡(h⁡(w𝒟)​(x,Tmax1))|∞≃4,032⋅10−3,\displaystyle\max_{x\in\Omega}\Big|v_{{\cal D}}^{k}(x,T_{\text{max}}^{1})-g(h(w_{{\cal D}})(x,T_{\text{max}}^{1}))\Big|_{\infty}\simeq 4,032\cdot 10^{-3},

whereas

maxx∈Ω⁡|u𝒟k​(x,Tmax2)−h⁡(w𝒟)​(x,Tmax2)|∞≃3,121⋅10−14,\displaystyle\max_{x\in\Omega}\Big|u_{{\cal D}}^{k}(x,T_{\text{max}}^{2})-h(w_{{\cal D}})(x,T_{\text{max}}^{2})\Big|_{\infty}\simeq 3,121\cdot 10^{-14},
maxx∈Ω⁡|v𝒟k​(x,Tmax2)−g⁡(h⁡(w𝒟)​(x,Tmax2))|∞≃1,84⋅10−13.\displaystyle\max_{x\in\Omega}\Big|v_{{\cal D}}^{k}(x,T_{\text{max}}^{2})-g(h(w_{{\cal D}})(x,T_{\text{max}}^{2}))\Big|_{\infty}\simeq 1,84\cdot 10^{-13}.

7 Appendix

The proof of the following result can be found in [8, Lemma 5.3 and Lemma 5.4].

Lemma 7.1.

Let (t(n))n∈ℤ(t^{(n)})_{n\in{\mathbb{Z}}} be a strictly increasing sequence of real numbers such that limn→−∞t(n)=−∞\lim_{n\rightarrow-\infty}t^{(n)}=-\infty and limn→∞t(n)=∞\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}t^{(n)}=\infty. Moreover, let tδ(n):=t(n+1)−t(n)t_{\delta}^{(n)}:=t^{(n+1)}-t^{(n)} be uniformly bounded. For all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} we denote by n⁡(t)n(t) an integer nn, such that t∈[t(n),t(n+1))t\in[t^{(n)},t^{(n+1)}). Let (a(n))n∈ℤ(a^{(n)})_{n\in{\mathbb{Z}}} be a family of nonnegative real values such that a(n)≠0a^{(n)}\neq 0 for finitely many n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}. Then, for all τ∈(0,+∞)\tau\in(0,+\infty) and ζ∈ℝ\zeta\in\mathbb{R}

∫ℝ∑n=n⁡(t)+1n⁡(t+τ)(tδ(n)​a(n+1))​d​t=τ​∑n∈ℤ(tδ(n)​a(n+1)),\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\sum_{n=n(t)+1}^{n(t+\tau)}\big(t_{\delta}^{(n)}a^{(n+1)}\big)\,\text{d}t=\tau\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\big(t_{\delta}^{(n)}a^{(n+1)}\big), (53)
∫ℝ(∑n=n⁡(t)+1n⁡(t+τ)tδ(n))​a(n⁡(t+ζ)+1)​d​t⩽(τ+maxn∈ℤ⁡tδ(n))​∑n∈ℤ(tδ(n)​a(n+1)).\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigg(\sum_{n=n(t)+1}^{n(t+\tau)}t_{\delta}^{(n)}\bigg)a^{(n(t+\zeta)+1)}\,\text{d}t\leqslant\big(\tau+\max_{n\in{\mathbb{Z}}}t_{\delta}^{(n)}\big)\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\big(t_{\delta}^{(n)}a^{(n+1)}\big). (54)

The following proposition is a direct corollary from Fréchet–Kolmogorov Theorem (see Brezis [2, Theorem IV.25, page 72]).

Proposition 7.2.

Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} be a bounded and open subset of ℝd+1\mathbb{R}^{d+1}, d=1,2d=1,2 or 33. Let (wn)n∈ℕ(w_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} be a sequence of functions wn​(x,t):ℝd×ℝ→ℝw_{n}(x,t):\ \mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, such that

  1. 1.

    for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, wn∈L∞​(𝒪)w_{n}\in L^{\infty}(\mathcal{O}) and there exists a constant Cb>0C_{b}>0 which does not depend on nn, such that ‖wn‖L∞​(𝒪)⩽Cb\|w_{n}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathcal{O})}\leqslant C_{b},

  2. 2.

    there exist positive constants C1,C2C_{1},\,C_{2} and a sequence of nonnegative real values (μn)n∈ℕ(\mu_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}, such that limn→∞μn=0\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mu_{n}=0 and

    ∫𝒪ξ,τ(wn​(x+ξ,t+τ)−wn​(x,t))2​d​x​d​t⩽C1​|ξ|+C2​τ+μn,\int_{\mathcal{O}_{\xi,\tau}}\big(w_{n}(x+\xi,t+\tau)-w_{n}(x,t)\big)^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}t\leqslant C_{1}|\xi|+C_{2}\tau+\mu_{n},

    for ξ∈ℝd,τ∈ℝ,n∈{0,…,N}\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\ \tau\in\mathbb{R},\ n\in\{0,\ldots,N\} and

     ​𝒪ξ,τ={(x,t)∈ℝd+1: the interval ​[(x,t),(x+ξ,t+τ)]​ lies in ​𝒪}. \rule{20.0pt}{0.0pt}\mathcal{O}_{\xi,\tau}=\big\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}:\text{\ the interval\ }\big[(x,t),(x+\xi,t+\tau)\big]\text{\ lies in\ }{\mathcal{O}}\big\}.\rule{20.0pt}{0.0pt}

Then there exists a subsequence of (wn)n∈ℕ(w_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}, denoted again by (wn)n∈ℕ(w_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} and a function w∈L∞​(𝒪)w\in L^{\infty}(\mathcal{O}) such that wn→ww_{n}\rightarrow w in L2​(𝒪)L^{2}(\mathcal{O}), as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty.

Lemma 7.3.

Let A>0A>0 and a function r⁡(s)r(s) satisfying

r∈C1(ℝ),r′(⋅)>0 on (0,+∞),r⁡(0)=0, and ​lim sups→0+s​r′​(s)r⁡(s)<∞\begin{split}&r\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}),\ r^{\prime}(\cdot)>0\text{\hskip 10.22217pton \hskip 10.22217pt}(0,+\infty),\\ &r(0)=0,\text{\hskip 10.22217ptand \hskip 10.22217pt}\limsup_{s\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{sr^{\prime}(s)}{r(s)}<\infty\end{split} (55)

be given.
Then there exists ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0 only depending on r⁡(s)r(s) and C>0C>0, depending only on r⁡(s)r(s) and AA, such that for all ε∈(0,ε0)\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0}) and for all u∈[0,A]u\in[0,A] the inequality

|ln⁡r⁡(u+ε)|⩽C⁡(|ln⁡ε|+1)\big|\ln r(u+\varepsilon)\big|\leqslant C\big(|\ln\varepsilon|+1\big)

holds.

Proof   Let α=lim sups→0+s​r′​(s)r⁡(s)+1\alpha=\displaystyle\limsup_{s\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{sr^{\prime}(s)}{r(s)}+1. There exists a constant ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0, such that for all s∈(0,ε0)s\in(0,\varepsilon_{0})

r′​(s)r⁡(s)⩽αs.\frac{r^{\prime}(s)}{r(s)}\leqslant\frac{\alpha}{s}. (56)

Let ε∈(0,ε0)\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0}) and u∈[0,A]u\in[0,A]. Then, either r⁡(u+ε)⩾1r(u+\varepsilon)\geqslant 1, which implies

ln⁡r⁡(u+ε)⩽ln⁡r⁡(A+ε0)\ln r(u+\varepsilon)\leqslant\ln r(A+\varepsilon_{0})

or r⁡(u+ε)⩽1r(u+\varepsilon)\leqslant 1. In that case

|ln⁡r⁡(u+ε)|⩽|ln⁡r⁡(ε)|,\big|\ln r(u+\varepsilon)\big|\leqslant\big|\ln r(\varepsilon)\big|,

holds. Integrating inequality (56) over the interval [ε,ε0][\varepsilon,\varepsilon_{0}], we obtain

|ln⁡r⁡(ε)|⩽|ln⁡r⁡(ε0)|+α⁡(|ln⁡ε0|+|ln⁡ε|).\big|\ln r(\varepsilon)\big|\leqslant\big|\ln r(\varepsilon_{0})\big|+\alpha\big(|\ln\varepsilon_{0}|+|\ln\varepsilon|\big).

Setting C=max⁡{α,α​|ln⁡ε0|+|ln⁡r⁡(ε0)|,ln⁡(r⁡(A+ε0))}C=\max\big\{\alpha,\,\alpha|\ln\varepsilon_{0}|+|\ln r(\varepsilon_{0})|,\,\ln\big(r(A+\varepsilon_{0})\big)\big\} we conclude the proof.  ■\blacksquare
